subject: Why upper limit on parameters changes the behaviour of the sampler?

messages.author: 7a97c986864bf6d6
messages.subject: Why upper limit on parameters changes the behaviour of the sampler?
parts:
Hello Community,

why upper limit changes the behaviour of the sampler? Shouldn't be simply a "limit"?


For example with the upper limit of   vector<lower=0.00001, upper=1000>[P] alpha[R];                


while for without limit vector<lower=0.00001>[P] alpha[R];       (notice the initial value of alpha)


Thanks!

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: Why upper limit on parameters changes the behaviour of the sampler?
parts:
Hi,
Default initialization is made in unconstrained space, and if you add constrains the unconstrained space changes and initial values change. In your plots the y axis limits are different with different constraints, and it's now only possible to see that initial values are different, but it's not possible to see whether there are any practical difference after warmup.

Also why lower=0.00001 instead of lower=0?

Aki

Thanks!

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Why upper limit on parameters changes the behaviour of the sampler?
parts:
On Thursday, March 2, 2017 at 12:22:13 PM UTC+2, Stefano wrote:
Often if I set lower=0 I get the warning that some parameter such as variance gets = 0 when it should be > 0 . s this index of a "bad" model?

Or indication of bad prior. Generallym instead of having an arbitrary hard lower limit (like 0.00001) or upper limit (100), it's better to use continuous prior which goes to zero when the parameter (like alpha in your case) goes to zero. Note that lower=0 is not arbitrary but logical limit if the parameter has to be positive.
 


Bw.
Stefano

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Why upper limit on parameters changes the behaviour of the sampler?
parts:
But it has a mode at zero. If you really need to keep values away
from zero, you need something like a lognormal that drives the density
to zero as the parameter approaches zero.

Or you need to reparameterize the model.

Initialization is random in (-2, 2) by default *on the unconstrained
scale*. For

real<lower=a, upper=b> x;

the inverse of the unconstraining transform is

a + (b - a) * inv_logit(y)

So when you initialize y to zero, that (b - a) / 2, so you initialize
around the middle of that interval.

The definite bounds like that on intervals can also bias estimates
relative to the unbounded approach as mass bunches up near
the boundaries. That also causes computational issues as the unconstrained
value heads off to + or - infinity.

- Bob
